design_detail: Retrospective, cross-sectional analysis of the baseline data of Project MATCH, a multisite randomized trial that matched people seeking treatment for alcohol problems to treatments (recruited 1991–1993 at nine US clinical research units; an outpatient arm recruited from the community by newspaper advertisements and from outpatient programmes, and an aftercare arm recruited from inpatient or day-hospital programmes). Ages at four drinking landmarks (first getting drunk regularly; first alcohol-related problems; first difficulty stopping drinking before intoxication, called loss of control; onset of the worst period of drinking) were recalled at baseline. Landmark ages, the intervals between successive landmarks, and the time from getting drunk regularly to first treatment (only for the 735 people for whom MATCH was their first treatment, so that first treatment is the treatment at which they were recruited) were compared between women and men in 2 (arm) × 2 (gender) × 5 (current-age quintile) between-subjects ANOVAs. A treatment sample, not a general-population sample.
can_establish: Whether, in this sample of US adults with DSM-III-R alcohol abuse or dependence who volunteered for a treatment trial, women recalled reaching drinking landmarks at later ages than men and recalled shorter intervals between some landmarks, and how these differences varied with current age.
cannot_establish: Whether women in general progress faster than men: people were sampled at treatment entry at similar ages, so intervals that end at treatment (and, in practice, at the worst period, reached at the same age by both sexes) are tied to the recruitment age; nothing was recorded as it happened; people who never sought treatment or were dependent on other drugs are not represented; and no biological or social explanation was measured.

sample.recruitment: Treatment-seeking volunteers for a randomized trial (Project MATCH), recruited over 2 years, 1991–1993, at nine clinical research units across the US. Outpatient arm (688 men, 264 women): recruited from the community through newspaper advertisements and from outpatient clinical programmes. Aftercare arm (619 men, 155 women): recruited from inpatient or day-hospital programmes in private, public and Veterans Affairs facilities. All were seeking treatment for alcohol problems (p. 253, Method › Subjects, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: DSM-III-R alcohol abuse or dependence; age 18 or over; willing to accept random assignment. Excluded: current dependence on drugs other than nicotine and marijuana (in the 90 days before enrolment, per the Discussion; a history of drug dependence was allowed), suicidal or psychotic patients, and people unable to name a contact for follow-up (p. 253, Method › Subjects, 2nd paragraph; p. 259, Discussion, 10th paragraph). The analysis sample was the 1,589 of 1,726 participants with all four landmark ages (p. 253, Procedure, 3rd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Analysis sample (Table 1, p. 254), women aftercare/outpatient vs men aftercare/outpatient: n 148/231 vs 576/634; mean age 41.7 (SD 12.17)/38.3 (10.70) vs 41.5 (10.68)/38.5 (10.51); employed 75/73% vs 82/87%; White 83/79% vs 80/81%; Black 13/9% vs 14/4%; more than 12 years of education 49/62% vs 51/54%; married or cohabiting 36/36% vs 37/48%; alcohol-dependent 97/98% vs 96/96%; SCID alcohol symptoms 6.5/5.9 vs 6.9/5.9 (maximum 9). Women were 24% of the analysis sample (editors' arithmetic). Mean current age by quintile, sexes combined: 26.6, 33.2, 38.2, 44.3 and 56.9 years (p. 254, Statistical methods, 2nd paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (baseline data). 137 of 1,726 enrolled (7.9%) lacked one or more landmark ages, almost always the two self-administered DrInC items near the end of a long questionnaire (p. 253). By the editors' arithmetic from p. 253 and Table 1: 40 of 419 women (9.5%) and 97 of 1,307 men (7.4%) were left out; 33 of 264 outpatient women (12.5%), 7 of 155 aftercare women (4.5%), 54 of 688 outpatient men (7.8%) and 43 of 619 aftercare men (6.9%). Included and excluded participants were not compared. The treatment analysis kept only the 735 people (46% of 1,589) for whom MATCH was the first treatment; their sex split is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: A treatment sample of trial volunteers, the kind of sample in which telescoping was first described, not a general-population sample. People were sampled at treatment entry and women and men entered at about the same age (Table 1), so a later start in women mechanically shortens any interval that ends at treatment entry; the worst period of drinking was also reached at the same age by both sexes (35.2 vs 35.0 years, Table 2). People who never sought treatment, people dependent on other drugs, and people with psychosis or suicidality are not represented. Grouping by current age means the youngest participants could only report landmarks at young ages and are a subset who reached treatment quickly, which the authors acknowledge (p. 258).

exposure.measurement: The groups compared are women and men (the paper uses 'gender' and does not separate biological sex from social roles), within study arm and current-age quintile. Landmark ages were self-reported at the baseline assessment: first problems and worst problems from questions in the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-III-R (SCID); drunk regularly (age at which the person first started getting drunk regularly) and loss of control (age at which the person first had difficulty stopping drinking before intoxication) from two items of the self-administered Drinker Inventory of Consequences (DrInC). Age at first treatment was the age at entry to MATCH for those for whom it was the first treatment. All timing was recalled; none was recorded as it happened (p. 253, Procedure, 2nd paragraph; p. 256).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not analysed: drinking amounts and patterns were not part of the analyses; severity is described only by SCID symptom counts (Table 1, p. 254).
exposure.polysubstance: Current dependence on drugs other than nicotine and marijuana was an exclusion; past drug dependence was allowed (pp. 253, 259). Other drug use was not described or adjusted for; the authors say the results may not apply to people dependent on several drugs (p. 259).

comparison.controls: Women compared with men within each study arm and current-age quintile; the treatment-interval analysis compared women and men among the 735 people for whom MATCH was the first treatment.
comparison.matching: None. Study arm and current-age quintile were factors in the ANOVA; no other characteristic was adjusted for, although men were more often employed and more often married or living with a partner (p. 254, Results › Subject characteristics, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Family history, childhood conduct problems, psychiatric comorbidity (raised by the authors as a possible explanation, p. 258), body size and composition, drinking quantity and other drug use were not measured or not used. Nothing was recorded before treatment entry.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The same drug-dependence exclusion applied to both sexes; other drug use not reported for either.

outcomes.instruments: Quick Screen interview (demographics); Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-III-R (SCID: count of alcohol dependence symptoms, age at first alcohol-related problems and at onset of the worst drinking period); Drinker Inventory of Consequences (DrInC: five domains of negative consequences, plus the two age questions). The full baseline battery took three sessions of 6 to 8 hours in all (p. 253, Procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: No reliability or validity data are given for the recalled landmark ages; the authors recommend test-retest validation and linking the questions to periods of life (p. 258, Discussion, 7th paragraph). The two DrInC landmarks are single questions whose interpretation may vary, as the authors note.
outcomes.operationalization: Telescoping was operationalized as later landmark ages but shorter intervals between successive landmarks in women. Intervals were differences between recalled ages taken in the average order of the landmarks, so negative values were possible; only 53% of participants reported the full assumed order (p. 254, Statistical methods, 1st paragraph; p. 256). Time to first treatment = age at entry to MATCH minus age at getting drunk regularly, for the 735 for whom MATCH was the first reported treatment (p. 256).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial: univariate tests at .05 divided by the number of variables in each set (four landmark ages; three intervals), with interpretation limited to effects significant in both the univariate and the multivariate analyses (p. 254, Statistical methods, 3rd paragraph); the multivariate results are not reported. Simple main effects within quintiles used error terms computed within each quintile and Dunn's procedure (p. 255); their statistics are not reported.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (self-report questionnaire and structured interview by research assistants who knew participants' sex).

analysis.effect_sizes: Means (SD), women vs men (Tables 2 and 3, pp. 255–256): age at getting drunk regularly 26.6 (10.35) vs 22.7 (8.96); first problems 27.5 (10.75) vs 25.0 (9.87); loss of control 29.8 (11.28) vs 27.2 (9.95); worst problems 35.2 (10.89) vs 35.0 (10.93). Gender main effects F(1, 1,569) = 83.62, 32.35 and 38.67 for the first three (p ≤ .001), ω² = .03, .01 and .01; no gender effect for worst problems. Intervals: drunk regularly to first problems 0.9 (5.53) vs 2.3 (7.04), F(1, 1,569) = 13.04, ω² = .01; first problems to loss of control 2.3 (6.12) vs 2.2 (7.08), no gender effect reported; loss of control to worst problems 5.5 (8.31) vs 7.8 (8.67), F = 20.95 (df printed as 1/1,589), ω² = .01. Drunk regularly to first treatment (n = 735): 11.6 (9.01) vs 15.8 (9.67), F(1, 715) = 44.5, ω² = .04. Editors' calculation, unadjusted standardized differences (women minus men, pooled SD): landmark ages 0.42 (drunk regularly), 0.25 (first problems), 0.25 (loss of control), 0.02 (worst problems); intervals −0.21, 0.02 and −0.27; time to first treatment about −0.43 to −0.47 (the sex split of the 735 is not reported, so the pooled SD is bracketed by the two group SDs).
analysis.covariates: Study arm and current-age quintile as factors, with all interactions; nothing else.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Secondary analysis of a trial's baseline data; no analysis plan for this question is cited.
analysis.selective_reporting: Multivariate test results, the simple-main-effect statistics by quintile, the cell sizes and SDs for the 735-person treatment analysis, and the similar results said to hold for first problems to first treatment (p. 258) are not shown. Arm × age-quintile interactions are given only as F values, described as not shown (pp. 255–256).
analysis.power: Not reported. 379 women in all, 66 to 85 per quintile; the treatment analysis has 735 people of unknown sex split.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 1,589 people entering alcohol treatment in a trial, women recalled reaching three of four drinking landmarks 2.5 to 3.9 years later than men but reached their worst period of drinking at the same age (35.2 vs 35.0 years). Recalled intervals were shorter in women from getting drunk regularly to first problems (0.9 vs 2.3 years) and from loss of control to worst problems (5.5 vs 7.8), but not from first problems to loss of control (2.3 vs 2.2); among 735 people in their first treatment, women reported a shorter time from getting drunk regularly to treatment (11.6 vs 15.8 years). Gender explained 1% to 4% of the variance (ω²), and the differences were minor or absent in the youngest current-age quintile and grew with age.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that "Telescoping is a relatively robust phenomenon in treatment-seeking alcoholics" and that women are more likely to progress faster through the landmarks (p. 252); the Discussion speaks of strong support (p. 257), recommends identifying women at the loss-of-control stage for intensive intervention and alerting women that they are more likely than men to develop alcohol problems and dependence rapidly (p. 259), and offers biological explanations (higher blood alcohol from body size and composition, gastric first-pass metabolism, organ toxicity, hormones) and social or psychiatric ones, none of which was measured (p. 258). Gaps: (1) because people were sampled at treatment entry at similar ages, the shorter time to treatment in women is largely the mirror image of their later age at getting drunk regularly: in the editors' reading of Figure 1, the men–women gaps in time to treatment by quintile (about 0.8, 2.0, 4.5, 7.7 and 6.5 years) are close to the gaps in age at getting drunk regularly in Table 2 (0.8, 1.8, 4.1, 7.1 and 7.1); the interval ending at the worst period, reached at the same age by both sexes, is affected in the same way; (2) the effects are small (ω² .01 to .04), which the authors acknowledge (pp. 255, 259), and absent in the youngest quintile, so 'relatively robust' overstates them; (3) alerting women in general extends a treatment-sample finding to all women; (4) the landmark ages were recalled, and only 53% of participants reported the assumed order. The limitations paragraph names the exclusion of people dependent on other drugs (p. 259) but not the selection at treatment entry.

timeline.event: Piazza, Vrbka and Yeager: telescoping studied across first drink, first intoxication, first drinking problem and first treatment; a gender difference only from first problem to first treatment (as described by Randall et al., pp. 252 and 258).
Blankfield, age-matched inpatient women and men in Australia: telescoping for some landmarks only in the older group (as described by Randall et al., pp. 253 and 257).
This study: Project MATCH treatment sample; shorter recalled intervals in women for two of three landmark pairs and to first treatment, concentrated in older participants.
Two pooled US general-population surveys do not find the full telescoping pattern; this study is cited as ref. 4 (as recorded on the library's card sc_keyes_2010).
US general-population analysis of cannabis use disorder cites this study among treatment-sample findings for alcohol (Khan et al., PDF pp. 2 and 6, read in this round).
Review cites this study for faster progression in women with alcohol problems and explains the discrepancy with population surveys by sample (as recorded on the library's card sc_mchugh_2018).
Critique places this study among larger samples with discrepant results and fewer telescoping effects (as recorded on the library's card sc_marks_2018).

replication.where_it_stands: The two descriptions of this study already in the library are each partly right: in the full text women had shorter recalled intervals for two of three landmark pairs and to first treatment overall (as Keyes et al. and McHugh et al. cite it), but the differences were small and minor or absent in the youngest participants (closer to Marks and Clark's reading). The general-population analysis in the library (keyes_2010) did not find the full pattern. Whether telescoping is a feature of women's drinking careers or of who reaches treatment, and when, remains open; no prospective test is cited here.

funding.funder: Acknowledgments: the authors thank the Project MATCH Research Group and the other people and institutions who collected the data, and are grateful to the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism for its support of this research; no grant number is given (p. 259).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Alcohol Research Center, Medical University of South Carolina (Randall, Roberts); Department of Psychology, University of South Florida (Del Boca); Substance Abuse Treatment Unit, Connecticut Mental Health Center, Yale University (Carroll); Research Institute on Addictions, Buffalo (Connors); National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (Mattson) (p. 252). No commercial interest is apparent.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective general-population cohort of young women and men followed from before regular drinking, with landmarks and treatment recorded as they happen, analysed with survival methods that separate the chance of reaching a landmark from the speed of getting there; or, in treatment samples, comparisons that do not end intervals at the recruitment visit, with body composition, psychiatric comorbidity and access to treatment measured so that sex and gender can be told apart.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Volunteers for a treatment trial, with exclusions (other drug dependence, psychosis, suicidality): suitable only for treatment-seeking people of this kind, not for the question of whether women in general progress faster.
Recruited by advertisement and from treatment programmes for a randomized trial, not sampled; how many were screened, eligible or declined is not reported in this paper.
1,589 people, but only 379 women (66 to 85 per quintile); the treatment analysis has 735 people of unknown sex split.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Table 1 by arm and sex; recruitment and setting described (pp. 253–254).

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: 92% of enrolled participants analysed; missingness higher among outpatient women (12.5%); included and excluded people not compared.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: The quantities analysed are recalled landmark ages from single questions (two from a self-administered questionnaire) with no reported reliability or validity; 47% of participants did not report the assumed order.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Same instruments in both arms and both sexes, delivered by trained and monitored research assistants (p. 253).

A factorial ANOVA with current-age quintiles handles age crudely; intervals ending at treatment entry are fixed by the sampling; nothing else was adjusted for; multivariate and simple-effect statistics are not shown; several printed p values do not match their test statistics.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Participation among those approached is not reported in this paper.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI has no overall algorithm; the editors' summary is high risk for the site's question (do women progress faster than men?). The descriptive numbers, recalled landmark ages and intervals by sex and current age in this treatment sample, are clearly reported in Tables 2 and 3. But the sample was selected at treatment entry, which ties the intervals ending at treatment (and, in practice, at the worst period) to the recruitment age and makes a shorter interval in women largely a restatement of their later start; all ages were recalled; the effects were small and absent in the youngest participants; and several statistics are inconsistent. The paper may be cited for what women and men entering this alcohol treatment trial recalled: later landmark ages in women, the same age at the worst period, and shorter recalled intervals for two of three landmark pairs and to first treatment, concentrated in older participants. It should not be cited as showing that women in general progress faster from drinking to problems or to treatment.

key_findings.finding: Project MATCH enrolled 1,307 men and 419 women seeking treatment for alcohol problems (1991–1993, nine US clinical research units): outpatient arm 688 men and 264 women, recruited by newspaper advertisement and from outpatient programmes; aftercare arm 619 men and 155 women, recruited from inpatient or day-hospital programmes. The analysis sample was the 1,589 with all four landmark ages: 379 women and 1,210 men.
key_findings.locator: Method › Subjects, 1st paragraph; Method › Procedure, 3rd paragraph (p. 253); Table 2, N column (p. 255)
key_findings.note: Table 1 (p. 254) gives the analysed cells: women 148 aftercare and 231 outpatient; men 576 aftercare and 634 outpatient.

key_findings.finding: Landmarks were recalled at baseline: ages at first alcohol-related problems and at onset of the worst period of drinking from the SCID interview; ages at first getting drunk regularly and at first difficulty stopping drinking before intoxication (loss of control) from two items of the self-administered Drinker Inventory of Consequences. Missing ages were almost always these two items, asked near the end of a long questionnaire.

Women and men entered treatment at similar ages (aftercare 41.7 vs 41.5 years; outpatient 38.3 vs 38.5); 96% to 98% of each group were alcohol-dependent. Men were more often employed (82% and 87% vs 75% and 73%; χ² = 21.66, 1 df) and more often married or living with a partner (χ² = 4.97, 1 df).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Subject characteristics, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The partner difference is printed with p ≤ .001, but χ² = 4.97 with 1 df gives p of about .03 (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: Mean recalled ages, women vs men: getting drunk regularly 26.6 (SD 10.35) vs 22.7 (8.96); first problems 27.5 (10.75) vs 25.0 (9.87); loss of control 29.8 (11.28) vs 27.2 (9.95); worst problems 35.2 (10.89) vs 35.0 (10.93). Gender effects F(1, 1,569) = 83.62, 32.35 and 38.67 (p ≤ .001) for the first three, with ω² = .03, .01 and .01; the authors call these small relative to total variation but, at 2.5 to 3.9 years, clinically meaningful. No gender effect for worst problems. Editors' calculation, unadjusted standardized differences: 0.42, 0.25, 0.25 and 0.02.

Gender differences in landmark ages depended on current age: Gender × Age Quintile F(4, 1,569) = 6.81 (drunk regularly), 4.37 (first problems) and 3.32 (loss of control), each ω² = .01. In the youngest quintile women vs men were 18.8 vs 18.0, 19.2 vs 18.8 and 20.6 vs 20.4 years; in the oldest, 37.8 vs 30.7, 39.2 vs 34.3 and 42.4 vs 37.5. Current age itself explained far more variance (ω² .25, .26, .30 and .43 for the four landmarks), because younger patients reported each landmark at younger ages.
key_findings.note: The Discussion says the loss-of-control interaction was not significant (pp. 257–258), and F = 3.32 with 4 and 1,569 df gives p of about .01, not ≤ .001 as printed (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: On average the landmarks came in the order drunk regularly, first problems, loss of control, worst problems (mean within-person ranks 1.6, 2.0, 2.7 and 3.7; order kept in 19 of 20 design cells by means and 18 of 20 by ranks), but only 53% of individual participants reported this order.
key_findings.locator: Results › Order of landmark events, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Recalled intervals, women vs men: drunk regularly to first problems 0.9 (SD 5.53) vs 2.3 (7.04) years, gender F(1, 1,569) = 13.04, p ≤ .001, ω² = .01; first problems to loss of control 2.3 (6.12) vs 2.2 (7.08), no gender effect; loss of control to worst problems 5.5 (8.31) vs 7.8 (8.67), gender F = 20.95, p ≤ .001, ω² = .01, with intervals lengthening with current age (3.6 years, SD 4.31, in the youngest quintile to 9.9, SD 12.66, in the oldest; age-quintile F = 16.60, ω² = .04).
key_findings.locator: Results › Progression through successive landmark events, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Table 3
key_findings.note: The error df for the loss-of-control to worst-problems ANOVA are printed as 1,589 (the sample size) instead of 1,569 (reporting issue). Editors' calculation, standardized differences: −0.21, 0.02 and −0.27.

key_findings.finding: Among the 735 people for whom MATCH was the first treatment, the time from getting drunk regularly to first treatment was 11.6 (SD 9.01) years in women vs 15.8 (9.67) in men: gender F(1, 715) = 44.5, p ≤ .001, ω² = .04; age quintile F(4, 715) = 48.41, ω² = .17; Gender × Age Quintile F(4, 715) = 3.76, p ≤ .005, ω² = .01. Simple-effect tests (statistics not given) found no gender difference in the youngest quintile and significant differences in the other four.
key_findings.locator: Results › Progression from drunk regularly to first treatment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The numbers of women and men among the 735 are not reported.

key_findings.finding: Figure 1 shows mean time from getting drunk regularly to first treatment by sex and quintile, without cell sizes or SDs. Editors' reading of a 300-dpi crop (approximate, to about 0.2 years), men vs women: quintile 1 8.0 vs 7.2; quintile 2 13.1 vs 11.1; quintile 3 16.2 vs 11.7; quintile 4 18.9 vs 11.2; quintile 5 25.0 vs 18.5. The men–women gaps (about 0.8, 2.0, 4.5, 7.7 and 6.5 years) are close to the gaps in age at getting drunk regularly in Table 2 (0.8, 1.8, 4.1, 7.1 and 7.1), as expected when first treatment is the recruitment visit and women and men of a quintile entered at similar ages.
key_findings.note: Figure values are approximate and are the editors' reading; Table 2 is for the full 1,589, not the 735.

key_findings.finding: No significant interaction of study arm with gender was found for any landmark age or interval, which the authors read as outpatients and aftercare patients showing the same pattern of gender differences.

The authors offer two explanations for the absent gender differences in the youngest participants, which their data cannot distinguish: the youngest patients are a subset of fast progressors whose speed masks differences, or social norms have changed so that both sexes now seek treatment earlier.

The authors acknowledge that some participants reported first problems before getting drunk regularly, possibly from different interpretations of the questions or recall bias, and recommend standardized landmark definitions, test-retest validation of the self-reports and questions linked to periods of life.

Possible causes are offered as hypotheses, none measured in this study: higher blood alcohol in women from smaller body size, more fat and less body water and possibly lesser gastric first-pass metabolism; greater organ toxicity (corticosterone findings in female rats, tissue penetration, receptor sensitivity); alcohol–estrogen interactions; sex differences in reward neurobiology; women being more readily identified as having alcohol problems; and more depression and anxiety in women.

The authors grant that the gender differences are small relative to total variation but call them clinically meaningful, recommend identifying women at the loss-of-control stage for intensive intervention, and say women should be alerted that they are more likely than men to develop alcohol problems and dependence rapidly.

Stated limitation: conclusions are limited to the Project MATCH sample, which excluded people dependent on drugs other than nicotine and marijuana in the 90 days before enrolment; whether telescoping occurs in people dependent on several drugs, on other drugs or not yet dependent is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: Two chi-square tests are printed with p ≤ .001 although their values give larger p: education by arm χ² = 7.41 with 1 df (p about .006) and living with a partner by sex χ² = 4.97 with 1 df (p about .03) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the differences in sample characteristics are less certain than printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The Gender × Age Quintile interaction for loss of control (F = 3.32, 4 and 1,569 df) is printed with p ≤ .001 and called significant in the Results (p. 255), but these values give p of about .01 (editors' calculation), and the Discussion states there was no significant interaction for this landmark (pp. 257–258).
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the age dependence of the loss-of-control difference met the authors' own rule (univariate at .05/4 and multivariate) cannot be determined; the multivariate results are not reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The ANOVA of the loss-of-control to worst-problems interval is reported with error df of 1,589 (F = 20.95, 1/1,589; F = 16.60 and 3.86, 4/1,589), equal to the sample size; with 20 design cells the error df should be 1,569, as in the other analyses.

Interpretation was to be limited to effects significant in both the univariate and multivariate analyses (p. 254), but no multivariate statistic is reported, and the simple-main-effect tests by quintile behind the statements that gender differences were absent in the youngest and present in the older quintiles are given without statistics (pp. 255, 257).
reporting_issues.consequence: The claims about which quintiles show a gender difference cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The treatment analysis of 735 people reports neither how many were women and men nor the cell sizes and SDs behind Figure 1; the Discussion also reports similar results for first problems to first treatment without data (p. 258).
reporting_issues.consequence: The precision of the treatment-interval comparison, and its unreported companion, cannot be judged.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the sample as 1,307 men and 419 women, but every analysis uses 1,589 people (379 women, 1,210 men); exclusions for incomplete landmark ages were more frequent among outpatient women (12.5%) than in the other cells (4.5% to 7.8%) (editors' arithmetic from p. 253 and Table 1), and included and excluded participants were not compared.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; a small, unexamined selection within the women's outpatient group.

reporting_issues.issue: Intervals were computed in the average order of the landmarks, so they could be negative, yet only 53% of participants reported that order (p. 256); mean intervals therefore mix people whose landmarks came in different orders.
reporting_issues.consequence: The mean interval between two landmarks is not the time between events experienced in that order for nearly half the sample.
